entry.title: The Contents of Perception
entry.summary: In contemporary philosophy, the phrase 'the contents of perception' means, roughly, what is conveyed to the subject by her perceptual experience. There will be a way these things look to you when you see them: they will look to have a certain shape, color, texture, and arrangement relative to one another, among other things. Your visual experience conveys to you that the piano has these features.

entry.title: Japanese Confucian Philosophy
entry.summary: In Japan, Confucianism stands, along with Buddhism, as a major religio-philosophical teaching introduced from the Eurasian continent at the dawn of Japanese civilization, roughly the mid-sixth century. Although originally a Chinese teaching, it spoke universally, especially when discussing people, or, more broadly, humanity, rarely contextualizing its ideas in exclusionist terms. When discussing human nature, Confucian philosophers, for example, referred to people without exception.

entry.title: Rationalism vs. Empiricism
entry.summary: In its most general terms, the distinction between rationalism and empiricism has been taken to concern the extent to which we are dependent upon experience in our effort to gain knowledge of the external world. Experience includes both sense experience, which comes through our five outward-directed sense modalities, and reflective experience, our conscious awareness of mental activities such as thinking, doubting, remembering, and reasoning.
